title: The dog and its reflection
hookLine: a dog drops its bone to grab the bigger one in the water (Aesop)

cards: It finally arrives, the thing you wanted: the phone, the apartment, the job. For about a week, it's wonderful. Then you see someone else's version.
A bigger one. A newer one. A better view.
And the thing in your hands, the one you were so glad about last Tuesday, suddenly feels small. Nothing about it changed. Only where you were looking.
The Greeks had a story for this, and it stars a hungry dog trotting home across a narrow bridge, with dinner in its mouth.

teach.h: MEAT, NOT A BONE, IN THE GREEK.
teach.b: In the picture books it's a bone. In the old Greek collections of Aesop, it's usually a piece of meat, a real prize for a dog.

He's carrying it home across a plank over a stream, or wading a river, depending on the version. He glances down. There in the water is another dog, with another piece of meat, and this one looks bigger.
So he does what hungry creatures do.

teach.h: HE SNAPS, AND DROPS HIS OWN.
teach.b: He opens his mouth to snap at the other dog's dinner, and his own piece drops, splashes, and is gone, carried off by the current. And the other dog? Gone too, because it was never there.

teach.h: THE BIGGER ONE WAS ONLY HIMSELF.
teach.b: The water had only shown him himself. He walks home with nothing. The old versions end with a moral about greed: grab for more, and lose what you had.
That's true, and it's plenty. But there's a second thing in the story that's easy to miss. The bigger dinner wasn't someone else's at all.
It was his own, seen in a different light, looking larger than it was. A lot of what people reach for works like that. Somebody's vacation photos.
Somebody's kitchen. Often it's your own ordinary life, reflected back with better lighting. The dog didn't need a bigger piece of meat.
He needed to notice the one already in his mouth. That sounds small, and isn't.
The Tao Te Ching says something close: whoever knows they have enough is rich. Aesop just says it with a wet, hungry, disappointed dog.

how: Readers of Aesop have long used the dog and its reflection to talk about greed and envy; people who keep a gratitude habit do something similar each day, naming what they already have.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: in the old Greek versions, the dog carries a bone
it's usually a piece of meat. the bone came later.
the bigger dinner in the water was the dog's own

games.q: you're the dog. you have dinner in your mouth, and below you in the water is a dog with a bigger piece. what do you do?
o: keep walking home with your own
bark to scare the other dog off
games.why: he snaps, and his own piece falls into the water and is carried away. the other dog was only his reflection. he goes home with nothing.

practice: If there's something near you that you use every day, a mug, a coat, your own two hands, hold it or look at it; if not, bring one to mind.

Notice it as if it had just arrived: its weight, its color, the ways it has helped you without being thanked. When your mind drifts to something you'd rather have, come back to this one: the piece in your mouth.

wordCard.voice: Aesop, whose fable tells of a dog who dropped his real dinner reaching for a bigger piece that was only his own reflection. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: dog. the fable comes down to us in Greek collections, and later in Latin verse.

carryVoice: Your line: hold what you have. The real one is the one you're holding. Day sixty-nine, in the books.
